common_name: Morex Barley (University of Minnesota Six-Row Malting Barley)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill as soon as the ground can be worked in spring; Morex is a six-row spring barley bred at the University of Minnesota and remains a reference variety for malting quality.

directions: Morex is a six-row spring barley developed by the University of Minnesota and has long served as the benchmark variety against which other malting barleys are measured for enzyme activity and extract yield. Drill into a firm, fertile seedbed as early in spring as the soil can be worked, since barley germinates in cooler ground than corn or sorghum and benefits from getting ahead of summer heat. The plant tillers readily and fills its heads with plump kernels well suited to malting for beer and whiskey as well as livestock feed. Harvest once the heads have dried to a uniform straw color and the kernels are hard, then store the threshed grain in a cool, dry space to preserve germination and malting quality.

common_name: Robust Barley (North Dakota Six-Row Malting Barley)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in early spring as soon as soil is workable; Robust is a six-row spring malting barley bred at North Dakota State University for the Upper Midwest.

directions: Robust is a six-row spring barley bred at North Dakota State University that became a widely grown malting standard across the Upper Midwest for its combination of yield and acceptable malting quality. Sow into a firm seedbed as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, since the crop needs a long cool stretch to fill its heads before summer heat sets in. It carries moderate straw strength and performs reliably under the dry, continental growing conditions of the northern Great Plains. Swath or straight-combine once the kernels are hard and the straw has turned from green to gold, then dry and store the grain to protect its malting value.

planting.note: Sow in early spring once soil is workable; Harrington is a two-row spring malting barley bred at the Crop Development Centre in Saskatchewan that became a dominant malting variety across the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies.

directions: Harrington is a two-row spring barley released by the Crop Development Centre at the University of Saskatchewan that, for a long stretch, was the most widely grown malting barley in Canada and much of the northern United States. It produces plump, uniform kernels prized by maltsters, along with short, sturdy straw that resists lodging better than many older two-row types. Drill into a firm seedbed early in spring, since it needs a cool start and a full season of moderate temperatures to fill its heads properly. Combine once the crop has dried down fully in the field, keeping harvested grain clean and well aerated in storage to preserve germination for malting.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Crop Development Centre

common_name: Conlon Barley (Upper Midwest Two-Row Malting Barley)

planting.note: Sow in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; Conlon is a two-row malting barley released by North Dakota State University for the Upper Midwest.

directions: Conlon is a two-row spring malting barley from North Dakota State University that gave growers in the Upper Midwest a shorter-strawed, lodging-resistant alternative to older six-row malting types. Drill into a firm, well-drained seedbed in early spring, since barley tillers and establishes best while the weather is still cool. The compact plant holds its head upright through wind and rain better than taller barleys, which helps keep grain quality high going into harvest. Combine once fully dry and store the kernels in a cool, well-ventilated space to protect their malting potential.

planting.note: Sow in early spring once soil is workable; Golden Promise is a short-strawed two-row barley originally bred in Scotland and long favored by distillers for single malt whisky.

directions: Golden Promise is a two-row spring barley developed in Scotland and best known for its long association with single malt Scotch whisky production, prized by distillers for the character it lends to new-make spirit even though it yields less than many modern varieties. Its notably short, stiff straw resists lodging well, which made it attractive to growers before semi-dwarf barleys became common. Drill into a firm seedbed in early spring and manage as a typical spring malting barley, giving it a cool start and avoiding excess nitrogen that can push protein content too high for malting specifications. Harvest once fully ripe and dry, and store the grain carefully to preserve germination for malting or distilling use.

common_name: Full Pint Barley (Oregon Hull-less Craft Malting Barley)

planting.note: Sow in early spring once soil is workable; Full Pint is a hull-less two-row barley from the Oregon State University barley breeding program, popular with small-scale craft maltsters.

directions: Full Pint is a hull-less two-row spring barley from the Oregon State University barley breeding program that has become a favorite of small-scale craft maltsters in the Pacific Northwest for the distinct, grainy flavor it brings to malt. Because the hull threshes almost completely free, the harvested kernels require little further processing before malting, which appeals to growers supplying local breweries and distilleries directly. Drill into a firm seedbed in early spring like other spring barleys, and manage moisture carefully since naked barley kernels are more exposed to weathering and pre-harvest sprouting than hulled types. Harvest promptly once mature and dry the grain well before storage to protect quality.
sources: Oregon State University Barley Breeding Program

common_name: Don Oat (University of Minnesota Tall Spring Oat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill as early in spring as the ground can be worked, or sow 6-8 weeks before fall frost for a winter-killed cover; Don is a tall, leafy spring oat from the University of Minnesota favored for straw and forage biomass.

directions: Don is a tall spring oat released by the University of Minnesota and selected for strong straw and forage production rather than for grain yield alone, making it a useful choice where growers want extra biomass for mulch, bedding, or hay. Drill or broadcast into a firm seedbed as early as the ground can be worked, since oats germinate in cool soil well ahead of warm-season grasses. In the North it can also be sown in late summer for a fall cover that winter-kills, leaving a mat of residue over winter. Mow or graze before seed set if biomass and weed suppression are the goal, or let it mature fully for a straw and grain harvest.

common_name: Saia Black Oat (Brazilian Winter Cover Oat)

planting.note: Sow 4-8 weeks before the first fall frost; Saia is a named black oat selection out of Brazil widely used across the southern United States for fall and winter grazing and cover.

directions: Saia is a named black oat selection that came out of Brazilian cover crop breeding work and has become a widely sold strain of Avena strigosa in the southern United States, chosen for vigorous fall growth and heavy biomass before winter. Drill or broadcast into a firm seedbed in late summer or early fall so plants establish a deep root system and dense canopy before cold weather slows growth. Where winters are cold enough it winter-kills cleanly, leaving a weed-suppressing mat of residue for spring no-till planting, while in milder zones it can be grazed or mowed repeatedly through winter. Terminate by rolling, mowing, or herbicide before seed set if volunteer regrowth is a concern.

common_name: Tifgrain 102 Pearl Millet (University of Georgia Grain-Type Pearl Millet)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past the last frost; Tifgrain 102 is a grain-type pearl millet hybrid bred at the University of Georgia for bird seed and feed-grain production.

directions: Tifgrain 102 is a grain-type pearl millet hybrid developed at the University of Georgia and selected specifically for seed production rather than forage, producing dense, well-filled heads popular for wild bird seed mixes and poultry feed. It tolerates heat and drought far better than corn and can be grown successfully on sandier, less fertile ground where other grain crops struggle. Sow into warm soil after all danger of frost has passed, since pearl millet germinates poorly in cool conditions. Cut whole heads once the grain has dried and hardened, then thresh and screen to separate the small round seed from the chaff.

common_name: Tifleaf 2 Pearl Millet (University of Georgia Leafy Dwarf Forage Millet)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is consistently warm; Tifleaf 2 is a leafy dwarf forage pearl millet hybrid from the University of Georgia bred ahead of the later Tifleaf 3 release.

directions: Tifleaf 2 is a leafy, dwarf-type forage pearl millet hybrid developed at the University of Georgia that established pearl millet as a serious warm-season grazing and cover crop before later Tifleaf releases extended the line. Its shorter stature compared to older tall pearl millet types reduces lodging and keeps more leaf relative to stem, which livestock and graziers both favor. Sow into warm, moist soil after the last frost, since establishment is slow in cool ground, and clip or graze repeatedly through summer to encourage leafy regrowth rather than letting it head out. As with other pearl millets, it carries no prussic acid risk, so frosted or stressed regrowth can be grazed without the caution required for sorghum-sudangrass.

planting.note: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; Quncho is an improved white-seeded teff variety released by Ethiopian national agricultural research and now one of the most widely grown teff varieties in Ethiopia.

directions: Quncho is an improved white-seeded teff variety released through Ethiopian national agricultural research that combined the preferred light seed color of older landraces with higher yield and better lodging resistance, and it has since become one of the most widely planted teff varieties in its home country. Mix the dust-fine seed with sand or dry compost for even broadcasting onto a firm, well-prepared bed, then roll or tamp rather than burying the seed deeply. The crop forms a fine-textured, airy stand that should be cut once most seed heads have dried, since mature teff shatters easily in wind or heavy rain. Dry the cut bundles thoroughly, then thresh and winnow in a light breeze to recover the tiny, nutrient-dense grain used for injera and other foods.

planting.note: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; Dessie is a brown-seeded teff variety grown commercially for grain in the United States.

directions: Dessie is a brown-seeded teff variety grown by US teff seed producers for grain, offering home growers another seed-color option alongside the ivory and standard brown types already common in cultivation. Blend the fine seed with sand or dry fertilizer before broadcasting onto a firm bed, then roll or tamp the surface instead of covering the seed with soil. Like other teff types it forms a fine, airy stand that fills out quickly in warm weather and should be watched closely as seed heads mature, since the tiny seed shatters readily once fully dry. Cut the stand when most heads have turned from green to tan, dry under cover, then thresh and winnow to recover the grain.

planting.note: Direct sow from a couple of weeks before to a couple of weeks after the last frost; Faro was bred at a Danish university for day-length neutrality and early maturity in short, cool growing seasons.

directions: Faro came out of the same Danish university quinoa breeding effort that produced other day-neutral, short-season lines, aimed at letting growers in northern Europe and similarly short-summer regions ripen a quinoa crop reliably before fall frost. It grows into a relatively compact, early-maturing plant, which helps it dodge lodging and late-season disease pressure compared to taller heirloom Andean types. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun around the last frost date and thin plants to give their seed heads room to bulk up. Harvest whole plants once the seed heads dry and rattle, then thresh and rinse thoroughly to remove the bitter saponin coating before cooking or storing the grain.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring around the last frost; Puno was among the first quinoa varieties successfully trialed outside the Andes in Colorado during early American efforts to adapt the crop.

directions: Puno was one of the original quinoa lines used in early Colorado field trials that first demonstrated quinoa could be grown successfully in North America outside its native Andean highlands, and it remains a useful reference variety for cool, high-altitude growing conditions. Direct sow into well-drained, average soil in full sun in early spring, since the plant tolerates light frost better than most warm-season grain crops. It grows tall with a prominent central seed head typical of Andean quinoa types, so stake or plant in blocks for mutual wind support in exposed gardens. Harvest once the seed heads dry and the grain rattles loose, then thresh and rinse well to strip away the bitter saponin coating before cooking.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
